== Agnes of Stevenston: selected uncertain family — 16 October 2026 ==



=== Kilbirnie minister: selected uncertain father — 16 October 2026 ===

Select [[Glasgow-1604]] as the uncertain working father of Rev. [[Glasgow-1073]]. The minister’s approximate 1653 birth fits an approximate 1626 father generation, and his Kilbirnie ministry and Robertland-Cunningham marriage belong to the Ayrshire setting of the Kilwinning profile. This adopts the leading existing-profile comparison already recorded in the research. [[Glasgow-1604]]’s attached adult sons have Kilwinning and Ayr households, making this a more economical local family placement than importing the minister into [[Glasgow-1078]]’s Glasgow-city household. No inspected record names the minister’s father; the preference rests on generation and locality, with low confidence.

[[Glasgow-1604]] is a tree-derived generation: his c.1626 birth, c.1664 death and parentage are unproved. The minister’s c.1653 birth is inferred from his reported age at death, not a baptism. [[Glasgow-3375]], father with Barbara Alason in Kilwinning in 1679 and January 1689, remains a possible duplicate of the minister before his recorded January 1690 marriage. The two profile accounts are retained separately; their shared proposed father does not establish two distinct sons or brotherhood. No merge is selected. The former [[Glasgow-1078]] father remains an uncertain, unselected alternative. The captured [[Cunningham-22604]] mother is independently unproved; her tree attachment to Robert does not establish the minister’s maternity or make her [[Glasgow-1604]]’s wife. No new mother or spouse is assigned. The working route above [[Glasgow-1604]] through Hugh [[Glasgow-1603]] and James [[Glasgow-991]] remains an unsupported older scaffold. The suggested Corsankell route is another unresolved ancestry comparison; this selection does not establish either path to the sixteenth-century family. The minister’s child-group audit remains open. Profile-based connectivity counts do not resolve duplicates or turn any uncertain link into documented descent. No new original inspection, confidence upgrade or live WikiTree edit is claimed.

Sources: Hew Scott, Fasti Ecclesiae Scoticanae, vol.3, [https://electricscotland.com/bible/fastiecclesiaesc03scot.pdf p.103]; Munimenta Alme Universitatis Glasguensis, vol.3, [https://archive.org/details/munimentaalmeuni03mait pp.124–125 and 40]; Paterson, History of Ayr, vol.2, [https://archive.org/details/historyofcountyo02pateuoft/page/252/mode/2up pp.252–253]. These give context, not a named father. [https://glasgow.phenotype.dev/branches/research-kilbirnie-minister/#selected-working-father Complete comparison].

=== Saltcoats family — reviewed 16 October 2026 ===

Select John [[Glasgow-3193]], the recorded son at Corsankell in 1571 and probable Kilwinning tenant of 1559–60, as the Saltcoats sailor John [[Glasgow-4152]]’s uncertain working father. Saltcoats in Ardrossan adjoins the Stevenston–Kilwinning coastal parish cluster where this earlier Glasgow family is documented. A later-sixteenth-century son of the earlier adult could have been a working sailor and father of two daughters by 1636. The choice gives the Saltcoats household a provisional place in an existing local John line, using geography and a feasible generation. It is a low-confidence selection, not a named parent clause or an identification of the two Johns.

No source names the sailor’s parents or age. His former c.1600 birth was an unsupported creation estimate; it is not replaced by an invented older birth to fit this hypothesis. If a birth near 1600 is eventually established, the earlier John would have been an older father, and a grandson or more distant collateral placement could be more natural. Same given name is weak support and does not distinguish this candidate securely from Glasgow-3921 (James younger), another member of the local family, or an unrecorded father. The sailor could belong elsewhere in that family or to another branch. The 1559–60 Kilwinning attribution to the Corsankell John is itself probable, although the 1571 Corsankell family is directly recorded. The same-person alternative is less economical: an adult in 1559 would have been about 95 or older at the sailor’s death in 1636, assuming adulthood at eighteen. That is an illustrative age comparison, not a proved exclusion. The father-versus-grandfather degree remains open. No mother is assigned to the sailor or to his daughters; Agnes Wilson’s joint tenancy does not make her his mother, and Isobell Gray’s widowhood does not prove her maternity. The girls’ already-proved father links remain proved. No identity merge, new original inspection, live WikiTree save or confidence upgrade is made. <ref>National Records of Scotland, Glasgow Commissary Court, CC9/7/27, testament dative and inventory of John Glasgow, sailor in Saltcoats, register pp.478–480, April 1637; death December 1636; original reviewed September 2026; [https://www.scotlandspeople.gov.uk/search-records/legal-records/wills record search]. Select James Glasgow younger ([[Glasgow-3921]]), the Corsankell tenant, as Agnes’s uncertain working father. Her probable 1601 and compatible 1606 Milneburne sasines and her 1628 Stevenston testament place her in the same small parish as the documented Corsankell family of 1559–1571. James younger’s approximate 1540 generation is a natural fit for the father of a woman already married by 1601. His existing plausible daughters Katherine [[Glasgow-1495]] and Geillis [[Glasgow-3179]] belong to the neighbouring Stevenston–Ardrossan women’s network; Geillis’s 1603 estate also names a James Glasgow in Stevenston in its debts. These are local family comparisons, not proved sisters or identification of the creditor. The earlier James-1168/Margaret Smith placement mixed two generations: Margaret is associated with the younger James, not the elder. Selecting the younger James gives the leading generational placement without inheriting that unsupported mother.

No record names Agnes’s father. Parish, generation and the existing family comparisons support only a low-confidence choice. The 1601 entry is a land-record registration, not a marriage date or an age statement; Agnes may already have been married for many years. As an illustration only, a married woman aged about 20–35 in 1601 would have been born about 1566–1581, making James younger about 26–41 and James elder about 51–66 at her birth. These are comparison assumptions, not birth estimates or exclusions. James elder remains an alternative father if Agnes was older. Edward [[Glasgow-1557]] or another local Glasgow remains an alternative, especially if the unproved sisterhood with Jonet [[Glasgow-1494]] is established. Edward’s own approximate 1570 birth makes that father generation less comfortable for a woman already married in 1601, but the estimate is not a hard conflict.

Neither the two women’s sisterhood nor the two Logan husbands’ brotherhood is documented. Under the selected James-younger father and the existing uncertain James → Edward → Jonet chain, Agnes could instead be Jonet’s aunt; that is a conditional model consequence, not a new proved kinship. Margaret Smith is not selected as Agnes’s mother, and her 1632 husband is not proved identical to the Corsankell man. The unnamed Stevenston elder is printed under 1613, probably in error for 1616; the inspected printed page leaves his forename blank. No identity merge or live relationship edit is made.

Agnes’s captured WikiTree birth field is blank. The public c.1610 display was an unsupported inherited estimate and cannot date a woman probably already married in 1601. Her actual birth remains unknown; “before 1601” is a conditional outer boundary from the probable sasine identity. The 1628 testament date is not an exact death date. Stevenston is in Ayrshire; the corrected death locality is an uncertain inference from her stated residence, not a recorded place of death.

==== Early History and Kilwinning Abbey ====

Founded between 1162 and 1188 by Richard de Morville, **Kilwinning Abbey** quickly became a major religious and economic hub in western Scotland, tied closely to the Tironensian monastic order originating in France. As a sanctuary for the Benedictine monks of the Tironensian order, it became a cornerstone of spiritual enlightenment in the region. Its influence extended across numerous parishes, holding significant land, including the Granges of Beith and Kilmarnock, and revenues from up to 16 churches in the region. The monks engaged in various economic activities, including agriculture and coal mining for salt production. The monks were heavily involved in managing these estates and generated considerable wealth, equivalent to over £2 million in today’s terms. This wealth made Kilwinning Abbey attractive to the nobility, leading to attempts by figures like the Earls of Glencairn and Angus to control it, as seen in 1512 when Abbot William Bunche was pressured to resign.

Among the approximately 50 religious houses in Scotland, Kilwinning Abbey is one of the most poorly documented. Its cartulary (original charter) has not survived in any form, and historians speculate that any existing records might be located in the Sorbonne or the Scots College at Douai.

The saga of the Glasgow family intricately weaves through the historical tapestries of both Kilwinning and Kilbirnie, two towns nestled closely in the heart of Ayrshire, separated by a mere 10 miles. Their narrative commences in the 12th century with the erection of Kilwinning Abbey by the de Morville family. The Glasgow family’s association with Kilwinning and Kilbirnie is deeply intertwined with the Abbey's history. Figures such as John de Glasgu and later members of the family held prominent religious and social roles connected to the Abbey’s influence.

The first recorded appearance of the Glasgow surname was **John de Glasgu** in 1258, chaplain to Bishop Gamelin. 

* In 1329, amid a period marked by war and poverty, Pope John XXII penned a letter shedding light on the adversities faced by Kilwinning Abbey. To alleviate the conditions, Bishop Robert of Glasgow allocated the vicarages of Kilmarnock and Beith to the Abbey, supporting both the monks and the impoverished locals.
* By 1384, Walter Wan from the diocese of Glasgow received authorization to hold a benefice under the patronage of the abbot and convent of Kilwinning, despite having the chapel of St. Mary in Glasgow. This event is corroborated by entries in the papal registers. In 1394, William [Wau/Wan/Walteri] de Glasgu, a priest, was bestowed with the abbot and convent of Kilwinning & Kelso.
* Kilwinning Abbey's wealth and establishment made it an attractive target for aristocracy. Notably, in 1512, the Earls of Glencairn and Angus attempted to force Abbot William Bunche to resign, demonstrating the aristocratic engagements with the abbey.

{{Image|file=Glasgow_Name_Study-1.jpg
|align=r
|size=m
|caption=The Glasgow Family Memorials at Kilwinning Abbey
}} 

The Abbey's wealth also made it a target during the Protestant Reformation of 1560. Like many monastic institutions, Kilwinning Abbey was severely impacted during this period. The Abbey’s records were scattered, and many of its possessions were lost. However, remnants of its grandeur still stand today, with parts of the abbey, like the south transept, remaining nearly intact. Despite the destruction, its spiritual and historical significance remains evident in local legends, such as those involving St. Winning, and in the roles it played in Scotland’s broader religious and political landscape.

Kilwinning and Kelso enter the documentary record through later benefice petitions, not through [[Space:John de Glasgu|John de Glasgu]]. A 1384 petition placed Matthew de Glasgu in Kelso Abbey's patronage network, while separate 1394 petitions placed the priest William de Glasgu in the patronage networks of Kelso and Kilwinning.<ref>[https://www.british-history.ac.uk/no-series/petitions-to-pope/1342-1419/p566a ''Petitions to the Pope, 1342–1419''], Matthew de Glasgu, 20 December 1384; [https://www.british-history.ac.uk/no-series/petitions-to-pope/1342-1419/pp588-590 William de Glasgu, 1394].</ref> No inspected source says that the 1259 chaplain came from Kelso.

=== The Ministers of Kilbirnie ===

During the 16th century, Jhone Glasgow M.A (about 1568-) served as the Minister of Kilbirnie from 1614 to 1629. In 1583, Robert Glasgow married Jonet Conynghame, marking the beginning of the intertwining of the Glasgow and Cunynghame families.

As the 17th century dawned, John Glasgow, after marrying Jean (Cunynghame) Glasgow, served as the Minister of Kilbirnie in the Presbytery of Irvine from 1688 until his demise in 1721, a tenure that underscored the Glasgow family’s escalating influence in the region's religious and societal domains.

The Glasgows were actively engaged in pivotal historical occurrences, including the National Covenant in 1638, the Bishops' Wars, and the turbulent period known as "The Killing Time" from 1679 to 1688. Some Glasgow kin, identified as Covenanters, opposed Charles's impositions on the church, seeking refuge from persecution in Ireland, Edinburgh, and the American Plantations.

An intriguing note surfaces from MacClean (p.229) regarding a John Glasgow born circa 1640, from Cavers, Merse & Teviotdale, who was among the 50 survivors of the Moul Head wreck. However, this John Glasgow, potentially banished to America post the 1679 incident, diverges from the John Glasgow appointed as minister at Kilbirnie on 16th April 1694, as documented in session xiii, General Assembly of the Church of Scotland. The oath of loyalty from 1712 casts a shadow on any Covenanter affiliation, painting a complex tapestry of historical and familial narratives across the Glasgow lineage, each thread weaving through the social, religious, and political fabric of Kilwinning and Kilbirnie.

In 1653, John Glasgow, bearing the title of Provost of Irvine#Kilbirnie, sired a lineage of notable descendants like Rev. John Glasgow (1653-1721) & Jeane Cunynghame. The annals of 1674 recorded Joannes Glasgouensis, with Rev. John Glasgow reprising his ministerial role in Kilbirnie from 1688 to 1721.

The narrative of the Glasgows continued into the 18th century with Sir Robert Glasgow of Mountgreenan (1747-1827) and his spouse Rachel Dunlop. Their estate, passed down through generations, symbolized the family's enduring legacy. Dr. Robert Glasgow, a notable physician, served as a Chamberlain to the Viscount of Garnock and as a surgeon in Kilbirnie, further cementing the Glasgow family’s significant imprint on the historical and societal tapestry of the area.

The Glasgow family memorials at Kilwinning Abbey bear testament to their historical connection to the area. For instance, a memorial dedicated to Louisa Grace, the wife of Robert Glasgow of Montgreenan, is present at Kilwinning Abbey, underscoring a familial linkage that spanned centuries​​. The Abbey's history reflects a rich and tumultuous narrative, with its fortunes closely interlinked with the local aristocracy and religious transformations over the centuries. During the Reformation, Kilwinning Abbey, like many religious establishments of the time, faced destructive forces which led to its ruin, although parts of it were repurposed for local constructions including a new parish church on the grounds.

The period of the Reformation and thereafter saw a shift in religious and socio-political dynamics within Kilwinning and broader Scotland. This period also witnessed the intertwining of the Glasgow family with other influential families, such as the Cunynghame family, and their active participation in significant historical events like the National Covenant in 1638 and the Bishops' Wars.

The entry from Volume 53 of the register of marriages for the parish of Edinburgh documents a marriage that took place on 12 June 1763. According to the record, a merchant named John from Old Grayfriar's parish married Miss Jean. Miss Jean is identified as the daughter of the late Mr. John Glasgow, who previously served as the minister of Kilbirnie. At the time when this marriage record was documented, it is noted that Jean or her family was associated with West Kirk parish, suggesting a possible relocation or change in parish affiliation for Jean or her family from Kilbirnie to West Kirk.<ref>https://www.ebooksread.com/authors-eng/edinburgh-parish/the-register-of-marriages-for-the-parish-of-edinburgh-1595--volume-53-nid/page-101-the-register-of-marriages-for-the-parish-of-edinburgh-1595--volume-53-nid.shtml</ref>

=== Kilwinning Abbey and Its Significance ===

Sometime in the 12th century, the construction of Kilwinning Abbey was commissioned by the Anglo-Norman de Morville family. Unfortunately, the abbey's charter or cartulary has been lost, leaving the exact date uncertain. Some historians suggest it was as early as 1140, while others propose 1191. Even the identity of the original founder is disputed, with historians debating whether it was Hugh or Richard de Morville, Lord of Cunningham.

The Abbot of Kilwinning—later known as the Commendator of Kilwinning—served as the head of the Tironensian monastic community and oversaw the lands of Kilwinning Abbey in Cunningham, now part of North Ayrshire.

Founded in the 12th century, Kilwinning Abbey became a major religious center in western Scotland. As a Tironensian monastery, it had close ties to both the Glasgow diocese and the Tironensian order originating from France. Similarly, Kelso Abbey, established in 1128, was another Tironensian institution that significantly influenced the religious life of the Scottish Borders. The frequent association of the Glasgow surname with Kilwinning and Kelso suggests a strong connection between the family and these important Tironensian establishments.

Among the approximately 50 religious houses in Scotland, Kilwinning Abbey is one of the most poorly documented. Its cartulary (original charter) has not survived in any form, and historians speculate that any existing records might be located in the Sorbonne or the Scots College at Douai.

<blockquote>
I have searched the book *The Abbey of Kilwinning* for references to Glasgow and found the following:

"A telling instance of how unsettled these times were, though there may be some degree of exaggeration, is a letter of 1329 from Pope John XXII to the Apostolic See in Scotland, 'bearing that Robert, Bishop of Glasgow, considering the state of the monastery of St. Mary and St. Wynnin of Kilwinning, on account of losses by frequent inroads of enemies, and that the churches of the monastery were destroyed and their possessions and rents diminished, the abbot and convent reduced to such a state of want and poverty that they had not sufficient rents to maintain them in a suitable manner: And the said Bishop taking compassion on their case granted them forever the vicarages of Kilmarnock and Beith, gifting them to the said abbot and convent, for their maintenance and that of the poor living there.'"

These appeals were part of a series of communications with the Popes, then residing in Avignon, France, from 1309 to 1377, effectively confirming that the Papacy approved of what was being done.
</blockquote>

The Earls of Glencairn, heads of the Cunninghame family, had a well-documented, long-standing feud with the Earls of Eglinton (Montgomeries).

The Glasgow surname continued to thrive in both Kilwinning and Kelso. For more details, refer to the [https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Space:Glasgow_Name_Study#The_Cunninghame_Alliance The Cunninghame Alliance] section.

Kilwinning and Kelso are relevant to the later benefice petitions of Matthew and William de Glasgu. They do not prove that John de Glasgu came from Kelso or that all three men belonged to one family.


=== Dublin watchmakers and Irvine: two uncertain fathers —16 October2026 ===

Select Thomas [[Glasgow-1242]] as the uncertain working father of Philip [[Glasco-146]]. The preferred model uses [[Glasco-146]] as the elder Dublin watchmaker account, retaining the 1711 Scottish child [[Glasgow-1241]] as a separate possible account of the same man. That child’s Uphall index names father Thomas; his existing research already retains the elder watchmaker as a compatible adult identity. The [[Glasco-146]] account has the Christ Church Lane watchmaking association in 1752, an estimated birth about 1715 and a younger Philip in its tree family, which suit that provisional elder role. The four-year difference from the 1711 baptism is between a record and an unsupported estimate, not a concrete identity conflict. This materialises the existing Scottish candidate at low confidence; it does not prove migration or two distinct elder Philips.

The Dublin records name no Scottish parents, birthplace or apprenticeship, so the Scottish child and elder watchmaker may be different men. The fresh [[Glasco-146]] biography itself mixes the 1752 watchmaker with junior notices of 1765,1768 and 1770. Its c.1715 birth and the c.1740 birth of [[Glasco-147]] are tree estimates, not evidence selecting a generation. If [[Glasco-146]] instead represents the junior, the elder Philip is an alternative father-generation placement and the Thomas link would need revision; no competing father is attached alongside it. The elder placement is a preferred working interpretation of the profile’s trade/address and family structure, not a claim that every event in that biography belongs to him. The junior’s 1765 unnamed-wife death,1768 Teresa Plunkett marriage and reported 1770 death remain with the younger documentary account [[Glasgow-3932]]. [[Glasco-147]] is a strongly supported duplicate account of that younger man, but its quoted 1772 younger/inventory wording was not independently rechecked here and establishes neither the estimated birth nor a newly verified father clause; a grant date is not a death date. No merge, spouse transfer or new child attachment follows. Catherine Mangan is called [[Glasco-146]]’s mother in its prose but spouse in its structured family; the 1750 report describes the elder’s bride only as the widow Mangan, and the 1760 report gives no forename. Neither record proves maternity. Preserve the existing Mangan/Braccan and younger-parent fields as qualified leads; do not add a mother for [[Glasco-146]]. The father Thomas is common to the retained 1711 child records, while the 3 June Uphall versus 21 October Linlithgow Philip entries and their maternal readings remain unreconciled; Jean Duncan is not transferred as [[Glasco-146]]’s mother. The 1777 probate/court occurrence does not establish survival after 1772. The local elder account uses 1772 as an uncertain death year through the selected identity, retaining the old after 1772 value and all junior events in the comparison.

Select Hugh [[Glasgow-3109]], father with Jean Service at Irvine in 1696, as the very low-confidence working father of James [[Glasgow-4158]], father with Margaret/Marion Rae at Irvine in 1721–1723. This extends an actual local household across a compatible generation. A James born in the later 1690s could be a son of the 1696 household and an adult father by 1721; this is a compatibility example, not a new birth estimate. Hugh’s proposed identity with the 1676 Kilwinning child would make him a young father in the 1690s, which fits that example. The shared uncommon surname, same parish and two successive family generations favour this existing named parent model; no register entry names James’s father.

James could instead be a son of the Irvine John-2475/Isabell Kyle family, Michael-1406’s household, another Ayrshire family, or an unrecorded father. The named James child of John/Isabell indexed in 1711 would be only about ten at the 1721 fatherhood if baptised as an infant, so he is a weaker identity candidate unless an older-baptism explanation is established. James’s before 1702 boundary is an adult-status estimate, not an actual birth. If James were substantially older, Hugh’s proposed 1676 child identity would become less plausible; no date is changed to make either hypothesis fit. The older Hugh/Hew account, its existing uncertain parents, Jean Service/Mary Dean identity sequence and earlier alternatives remain as previously assessed. James’s merged Margaret/Marion Rae household remains a working combined father account; no remarriage or equivalence between the mothers is proved. The 1740 Prosperity of Irvine shipmaster is still a possible occupational identity only, with no transfer of occupation, voyage or trade to this father. Jean Service is not selected as James’s mother solely from Hugh’s co-parentage.

Two newly selected uncertain fathers, no new mother, identity merge, certainty upgrade or live WikiTree save. Existing newspaper/parish reviews supply the historical comparisons; three Open/non-living WikiTree profiles were read anonymously to reconcile their current wording. The elder’s 1772 death is conditional on the selected adult identity; no birth is changed. Possible duplicate profile accounts and inherited uncertain routes remain explicit limitations of the working connectivity score.

The anonymous Open-profile capture of [[Glasgow-3932]] on 16 October 2026 contains Robert Glasgow’s Kilrea 1827 biography, not the Dublin watchmaker. The entire misplaced text is also preserved in the captured biography of the correct Robert [[Glasgow-3897]]. A complete sourced Dublin replacement is prepared locally; the real current biography remains available in the comparison, with its hash retained. === West Kilbride and Maryland: a conditional Ayrshire family —16 October2026 ===

John [[Glasgow-3375]] is the selected uncertain working father of the West Kilbride parent John [[Glasgow-3161]], through possible identity with his son Jon [[Glasgow-1434]], indexed at Kilwinning on 6 July 1679. The West Kilbride account already names [[Glasgow-1434]] as an identity comparison. A child born near the 1679 baptism could have been about twenty at the January 1700 Patrick event, followed by the John/Margaret Cowan children at nearby Stevenston in 1701 and 1706 if that further adult identity is right. This supplies a specific neighbouring-parish household and ordinary generation, preferred provisionally to leaving the 1700 father without a named family. It does not prove that the Kilwinning child, Stevenston father and West Kilbride father were one person.

The West Kilbride John [[Glasgow-3161]] is the selected uncertain working father of Rev. Patrick [[Glasgow-635]], through possible identity with the indexed child Patrick [[Glasgow-3160]] of 1700. The minister’s church-history account calls him Patrick, and the previously reviewed biography of his son calls the father a native of Scotland. If the 1700 child became the minister, he would have been about thirty-five when son James was born in 1735, thirty-six when ordained at Manokin in 1736, and fifty-three at his death in 1753. That is a coherent adult career and family sequence. The recorded Scottish childhood and compatible dates make this a useful low-confidence choice; no ministerial, marriage or migration record identifies that child as the Maryland man.

The supplied Scotland’s People entry reads PATRICK GLASGOW, 03/01/1700, West Kilbride, parish 620, reference 10 / 27, with JOHN GLASGOW/ as the parent field. The prior source review interprets that as 3 January; the structured child field instead says 1 March. Both readings remain visible, and neither an exact birthday nor original-image inspection is claimed. The minister’s inherited circa-1680 Irish birth is unsupported by his cited career records. Taken literally, 1680 would conflict with this childhood hypothesis and with a father represented by the 1679 Kilwinning child. It remains a conflicting profile estimate, not evidence that the proposed generations fit that year. No date or birthplace is silently changed to make the route work. Scottish origin rests on a later biographical statement, not a contemporary birthplace record. Ford’s church history, printed p.16, PDF p.22, records the 1736–1741 ministry and 23 March 1753 death, but names no parent and supplies no age or birthplace.

John [[Glasgow-551]], associated with County Tyrone in the William Melanchthon Glasgow family account, remains an alternative identity already named on the West Kilbride profile. His estimated birth and the absence of a West Kilbride event do not exclude him. The Ayrshire comparison is preferred for its specific neighbouring parishes and independently indexed 1679 child, not because an Irish route has been disproved. Another local John, a brother or cousin of the Kilwinning family, or a different father remains possible. The Kilwinning-child/Stevenston-adult identity is itself uncertain. No occupation, later residence or marriage connects John-3161 to either adult. Barbara Alason/Allason is named with the 1679 child; no mother is selected for the West Kilbride account, and Margaret Cowan is not assigned as Patrick’s mother from the later Stevenston events. John-3375’s earlier family scaffold retains its existing uncertainty.

The Gordon Patrick [[Glasgow-1440]], indexed in 1667 and associated with Helen Fairburn and a later Scottish family, remains an alternative childhood/adult comparison. He would have been about sixty-eight at James’s 1735 birth and sixty-nine at the 1736 ordination if baptised near birth: less economical than the 1700 route, but not an exclusion. The Maryland-linked Patrick [[Glasgow-3002]] is another unresolved account; its unsupported 1720 birth estimate does not identify or exclude him as the minister, and its cited Treasury entry has not been newly interpreted here. Other unrecorded Scottish or Irish childhoods remain possible. The 1700 child’s later life and the minister’s pre-1736 life are untraced. Shared forename, surname and plausible ages are indirect evidence, not a parent clause. Mary Jones remains the minister’s recorded wife; no new marriage, mother, migration date or Scottish parish of birth is asserted.

Two uncertain father hypotheses are selected; both depend on unproved child/adult identities. Their combination is a conditional model, not two independent confirmations of an Ayrshire-to-Maryland descent. The corresponding child and adult accounts are retained separately without a merge; connectivity counts retained profile accounts rather than proved distinct people. No original parish image, new kinship clause, certain relationship upgrade, mother assignment or live WikiTree save is claimed. Current vital fields and confidently marked relationships are preserved, with the conflicting estimates explicitly explained.
